title: Requirements before boxes
summary: Functional and non-functional requirements, the clarifying questions that change the design, read/write ratios, and turning daily users into requests per second.

steps.title: Two kinds of requirement
body: Before you draw a single box, find out **what** the system must do and **how well** it must do it.
- **Functional requirement**: a thing the system does for a user. "Shorten a URL", "follow a user", "see my feed".
- **Non-functional requirement**: a quality the system must have while doing it. Latency, availability, durability, consistency, cost, security.
| Functional | Non-functional |
| Users can upload a photo | An upload of 5 MB finishes in under 3 s at p99 |
| Users see posts from people they follow | The feed loads in under 200 ms at p99 |
| A seat can be booked | A seat is **never** sold twice |
| Old links keep working | 99.95% availability; no link lost once created |
Non-functional requirements decide the architecture. Two systems with the same features look nothing alike
when one needs 100 requests per second and the other 1 million, or when one may lose a few writes and the other may not.
> **Tip:** in an interview, write both lists on the board in the first five minutes. At work, they are the
> "Goals" and "Non-goals" of the design doc.

steps.prompt: Sort each requirement for a chat app.
items: Send a message to a group
Messages arrive in under 500 ms at p99
No acknowledged message is ever lost
Survive the loss of one data centre zone
Cost under $0.01 per user per month
steps.explain: Features are functional. Speed, durability, availability and cost are qualities: non-functional. The second list is what forces caches, replication and multiple zones.

steps.title: Questions that change the design
body: Each good clarifying question removes a whole family of designs. Ask them before estimating.
| Question | Why it matters |
| How many users, daily active? | Sets QPS, storage, and whether one database is enough |
| What is the read/write ratio? | 100:1 reads says *cache and replicate*; 1:1 says *partition the writes* |
| How big is one item? Does it grow? | Decides database rows vs object storage, and bandwidth |
| How fresh must reads be? | Strong consistency costs latency; seconds of staleness buys caches and replicas |
| What may we lose, and for how long may we be down? | Durability and availability targets (RPO and RTO) |
| Who are the users, where are they? | One region or many; mobile networks; CDN |
The **read/write ratio** is the single most useful number. A URL shortener reads a link hundreds of times for
every write. A metrics pipeline writes almost everything and reads a tiny summary. They need opposite designs.

steps.prompt: The interviewer says: "Design a URL shortener." What should you ask **first**?
options: Roughly how many links are created per day, and how many redirects? Do links expire? Can users pick custom aliases?
Should we use Cassandra or PostgreSQL?
Which hash function should we use for the short code?
Should the service run on Kubernetes?
explain: Scale, the read/write ratio and the features come first, because they decide everything else. Database,
hash and platform choices are answers; asking about them first means you have picked a solution before

steps.prompt: Match each answer from the product owner to the design decision it drives.
pairs: Cache hot items and add read replicas
Store blobs in object storage, not database rows
Strongly consistent writes with a transaction
A CDN and possibly several regions
"Stale counts for a few seconds are fine"
steps.explain: Every answer removes options. That is why the questions come before the boxes.

steps.prompt: Put the first phase of a system design discussion in a sensible order.
lines: Clarify the functional requirements (what it does)
Agree the non-functional targets (latency, availability, consistency)
Estimate the scale: QPS, peak, storage, bandwidth
Deep dive into the riskiest part
steps.explain: You cannot estimate before you know the features, and you cannot draw a sensible design before you know the scale. The deep dive goes where the estimates say the pressure is.

steps.title: From daily users to requests per second
body: A day has 86,400 seconds (call it 100,000 for mental maths, and say so). Average load is:
```text
average QPS = daily active users x actions per user per day / 86,400
peak QPS    = average QPS x peak factor          (2 to 3 for most consumer apps)
write QPS   = QPS x writes / (reads + writes)
Example: 20 million DAU, 10 feed loads each per day:
```text
peak (x3)                = about 7,000 QPS
Design for the **peak**, not the average: traffic follows the clock (evenings, Monday mornings, a
marketing email), and a system sized for the average is overloaded every single day.
- **Peak factor**: the ratio of the busiest minute's traffic to the daily average; measure it from real traffic when you can.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (`long` division truncates.)
steps.explain: 200,000,000 / 86,400 = 2,314.8, truncated to 2,314 by integer division. Times 3 is 6,942. In an interview, round to "about 2,300 average, 7,000 peak".

steps.title: Traffic from the requirements
prompt: Write three methods (use `double` arithmetic, no rounding inside):
- `double AvgQps(long dau, double actionsPerUser)`: `dau x actionsPerUser / 86,400`.
- `double PeakQps(long dau, double actionsPerUser, double peakFactor)`: the average times the peak factor.
- `double WriteQps(double qps, int readParts, int writeParts)`: the write share of `qps` for a read:write ratio
The tests round your results to compare them.
starter: double PeakQps(long dau, double actionsPerUser, double peakFactor)
double WriteQps(double qps, int readParts, int writeParts)
solution: double PeakQps(long dau, double actionsPerUser, double peakFactor)
double WriteQps(double qps, int readParts, int writeParts)
hints: The write share is `writeParts / (readParts + writeParts)`; multiply `qps` by it. Make sure the division is not integer division.
template: Dojo.Eq("one action per second exactly", 1.0, Math.Round(AvgQps(86_400, 1), 1));
Dojo.Eq("half an action per user", 0.5, Math.Round(AvgQps(86_400, 0.5), 1));
